text: A total lunar eclipse occurred at the Moon’s descending node of orbit on Tuesday, July 6, 1982, with an umbral magnitude of 1.7180, making it a central lunar eclipse in which part of the Moon passed through the center of the Earth's shadow. A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon moves into the Earth's shadow, darkening the Moon, and a total lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon's near side entirely enters the Earth's umbral shadow. Unlike solar eclipses, which are visible only in a small area, a lunar eclipse can be observed from anywhere on the night side of Earth. A total lunar eclipse can last up to nearly two hours, while a total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes at any given location due to the smaller size of the Moon's shadow. Occurring about 1.2 days after apogee (on July 5, 1982, at 2:30 UTC), the Moon’s apparent diameter was smaller. This was the longest total lunar eclipse since the 1859 eclipse. The eclipse was completely visible over western and central North America, western South America, and Antarctica, seen rising over northwestern North America, Australia, and the western Pacific Ocean and setting over northeastern North America, eastern South America, and west and southern Africa. It is part of an eclipse season, which occurs roughly every six months and lasts about 35 days, repeating every 173 days; each season typically includes two or three eclipses, separated by a fortnight, with the first and last eclipse in the sequence separated by one synodic month. This eclipse belongs to a semester series, repeating approximately every 177 days and 4 hours at alternating nodes of the Moon’s orbit. The penumbral lunar eclipses on March 1, 1980 and August 26, 1980 belong to the previous lunar year eclipse set, and those on May 15, 1984 and November 8, 1984 belong to the next set. It is part of Saros series 129, which repeats every 18 years, 11 days, and contains 71 events, beginning with a penumbral lunar eclipse on June 10, 1351. The series includes partial eclipses from September 26, 1531 through May 11, 1892; total eclipses from May 24, 1910 through September 8, 2090; and a second set of partial eclipses from September 20, 2108 through April 26, 2469, ending with a penumbral eclipse on July 24, 2613. The longest duration of totality occurred at member 37 on July 16, 2000, lasting 106 minutes and 24 seconds. All eclipses in this Saros series occur at the Moon’s descending node. Eclipses are listed in three columns, with every third eclipse in the same column being one exeligmos apart, meaning they cast shadows over similar parts of Earth. This eclipse is part of a tritos cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 135 synodic months (≈ 3986.63 days, or 11 years minus 1 month), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, though groupings of three tritos cycles (≈ 33 years minus 3 months) come close to having similar eclipses. It is also part of the long period inex cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 358 synodic months (≈ 10,571.95 days, or 29 years minus 20 days), with irregular appearances due to the same lack of synchronization, but groupings of three inex cycles (≈ 87 years minus 2 months) come close to having similar eclipses. A lunar eclipse is preceded and followed by solar eclipses by 9 years and 5.5 days (a half saros), and this lunar eclipse is related to two total solar eclipses of Solar Saros 136.
